{{Short description|Form of realism that suggests that mathematical entities are abstract}}
'''Mathematical Platonism''' is the form of [[Realism (philosophy)|realism]] that suggests that [[Mathematical entity|mathematical entities]] are abstract, have no [[spatiotemporal]] or causal properties, and are eternal and unchanging. This is often claimed to be the view most people have of numbers. 

==Overview==
The term ''[[Platonism]]'' is used because such a view is seen to parallel [[Plato]]'s [[Theory of Forms]] and "world of Ideas" (from Greek {{lang|grc|εἶδος}}, ''eîdos''), most famously described in his [[Allegory of the Cave]]: the everyday world, as perceived by the senses, only imperfectly approximates another—unchanging and ultimate—reality, which is accessible to the intellect alone. Both Plato's cave and Platonism have meaningful, not just superficial connections,{{Clarify|reason="connections to what? intuitively, to mathematics—but I am not sure that interpretation fits with the following adduction of Pythagoreanism as expansion/support."|date=August 2026}} because Plato's ideas were preceded and probably influenced by the hugely popular ''[[Pythagoreans]]'' of ancient Greece, who believed that the world was, quite literally, generated by [[number]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Calian |first=Florian |date=2015 |title=One, Two, Three? A Discussion on the Generation of Numbers in Plato's ''Parmenides'' |url=https://philarchive.org/rec/CALOTT-3 |journal=New Europe College |pages=49–78}}</ref>

A major question considered in mathematical Platonism is: precisely where and how do mathematical entities exist, and how do we come to know of them? If they exist independently of the mind—i.e., are not simply a human invention—is there some sense in which they can be said to occupy a separate, non-physical realm? If so, how is it that we are able to gain access to that world and discover truths about the entities therein?

One proposed answer is the [[Ultimate Ensemble]], a theory that postulates that all structures that exist mathematically also exist physically, in their own universes.

== Views ==
[[File:Kurt_gödel.jpg|thumb|[[Kurt Gödel]]]]
[[Kurt Gödel]]'s Platonism<ref name=SEP-P>{{Citation |last=Balaguer |first=Mark |title=Platonism in Metaphysics |date=2025 |work=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/spr2025/entries/platonism/ |access-date=2026-08-12 |edition=Spring 2025 |publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University |editor2-last=Nodelman |editor2-first=Uri}}</ref> postulates a special kind of mathematical intuition that lets us perceive mathematical objects directly. (This view bears resemblances to many things [[Edmund Husserl]] said about mathematics, and supports [[Immanuel Kant]]'s idea that mathematics is [[Analytic-synthetic distinction#Conceptual containment|synthetic]] ''[[A priori and a posteriori|a priori]]''.) [[Philip J. Davis]] and [[Reuben Hersh]] have suggested in their 1999 book ''[[The Mathematical Experience]]'' that most mathematicians act as though they are Platonists, even though, if pressed to defend the position carefully, they may retreat to [[Formalism (philosophy of mathematics)|formalism]].

=== Full-blooded Platonism<!--'Full-blooded Platonism' redirects here--> ===
'''Full-blooded Platonism'''<!--boldface per WP:R#PLA--> (closely related to, and sometimes used synonymously with, ''plenitudinous Platonism'')<ref name=SEP-P/> is a modern variation of Platonism, developed in reaction to the fact that different sets of mathematical entities can be proven to exist depending on the axioms and inference rules employed (for instance, the law of the [[excluded middle]] and the [[axiom of choice]]). It holds that all mathematical entities exist, so long as some self-consistent framework admits them; i.e., they need not all together be derivable from any ''single'' consistent set of axioms, since no such set is metaphysically privileged over alternatives.<ref>{{cite book| chapter-url = https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/platonism-mathematics/| title = "Platonism in the Philosophy of Mathematics", (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)| chapter = Platonism in the Philosophy of Mathematics| year = 2018| publisher = Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University| access-date = 2018-08-17| archive-date = 2018-11-25| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20181125182359/https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/platonism-mathematics/| url-status = live}}</ref> This has the benefit of providing a ready answer to [[Benacerraf's epistemological problem|Benacerraf's dilemma]]—if any consistent mathematical theory is guaranteed to pick out entities that actually exist, obtaining knowledge thereof poses no problem—though the view has faced criticism for thereby introducing an entirely new difficulty (a "uniqueness problem", wherein mathematical terms appear to lack determinate denotation; see "Platonized naturalism", below).<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Colyvan |first=Mark |last2=Zalta |first2=Edward N. |date=1999-10-01 |title=Mathematics: Truth and Fiction? |url=http://academic.oup.com/philmat/article/7/3/336/1440517 |journal=Philosophia Mathematica |language=en |volume=7 |issue=3 |pages=336–349 |doi=10.1093/philmat/7.3.336 |issn=1744-6406}}</ref>

=== Set-theoretic realism<!--'Set-theoretic realism' redirects here--> ===
Set-theoretic realism (also '''set-theoretic Platonism'''<!--boldface per WP:R#PLA-->),<ref>[[Ivor Grattan-Guinness]] (ed.), ''Companion Encyclopedia of the History and Philosophy of the Mathematical Sciences'', Routledge, 2002, p. 681.</ref> a position defended by [[Penelope Maddy]], is the view that [[set theory]] is about a single universe of sets.<ref>{{cite book| chapter-url = https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/naturalism-mathematics/| title = Naturalism in the Philosophy of Mathematics (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)| chapter = Naturalism in the Philosophy of Mathematics| year = 2016| publisher = Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University| access-date = 2018-08-18| archive-date = 2018-06-11| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180611125516/https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/naturalism-mathematics/| url-status = live}}</ref> This position (which is also known as '''naturalized Platonism'''<!--boldface per WP:R#PLA--> because it is a [[Metaphysical naturalism|naturalized]] version of mathematical Platonism) has been criticized by Mark Balaguer on the basis of [[Paul Benacerraf]]'s [[Benacerraf's epistemological problem|epistemological problem]].<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Balaguer | first1 = Mark | year = 1994 | title = Against (Maddian) Naturalized Platonism | url = | journal = Philosophia Mathematica | volume = 2 | issue = 2| pages = 97–108 | doi = 10.1093/philmat/2.2.97 }}</ref> 

=== Platonized naturalism<!--'Platonized naturalism' redirects here--> ===
A similar view, termed '''Platonized naturalism'''<!--boldface per WP:R#PLA-->, was later defended by the [[Stanford–Edmonton School]]: according to this view, a more traditional kind of Platonism is consistent with [[Naturalism (philosophy)|naturalism]]; the more traditional kind of Platonism they defend is distinguished by general principles that assert the existence of [[Abstract object theory|abstract object]]s. This formulation of mathematical Platonism is—as argued by proponents such as [[Edward Zalta]]—both proof against Benacerraf's dilemma in much the same way as is full-blooded Platonism, while yet escaping the "uniqueness problem" to which the latter has been alleged to be vulnerable.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Linsky | first1 = B. | authorlink2 = Edward N. Zalta | last2 = Zalta | first2 = E. | year = 1995 | title = Naturalized Platonism vs. Platonized Naturalism | url = | journal = The Journal of Philosophy | volume = 92 | issue = 10| pages = 525–555 | doi = 10.2307/2940786 | jstor = 2940786 }}</ref>
